--- title: "Synthesizing the literature" engine: knitr --- Literature synthesis asks what the collected studies establish about the concepts, processes, and relationships needed to understand the proposed study. The immediate goal is a set of evidence-linked synthesis notes that can be used to evaluate possible gaps. Begin with the papers and evidence recorded during [Searching the literature](literature_search.qmd). Read across those papers to identify areas of agreement, disagreement, qualification, and uncertainty. Return to searching when the available evidence cannot support or evaluate an important part of the emerging account. ## Identify the components of the explanation Begin with the literature-informed QHP. List the ideas needed to understand the proposed mechanism and expected relationship: 1. Which phenomenon or relationship needs to be explained? 2. Which mechanisms could explain it? 3. Which expected patterns follow from those mechanisms? 4. How have the central concepts been measured or represented? 5. Which places, time periods, organisms, and levels of observation have been studied? 6. Which organisms, systems, or contexts may affect the relationship? Use these questions to list the components needed for the explanation. A component may be a process, relationship, measurement problem, source of variation, or condition under which a relationship changes. Use these components to organize comparisons across studies. Their eventual relationship to paragraphs will be decided during outlining. ## Read across papers Use the literature-synthesis table and full-text notes from the search lesson. For each component of the explanation, compare the studies that inform it: - Which findings are consistent across studies? - Which findings conflict or vary among contexts? - Which studies test the proposed mechanism directly? - Which studies document only the expected pattern? - How does each study measure the relevant concept or process? - Which differences in design, place, time period, organism, or level of observation could explain different results? - Which assumptions connect the measurements to the authors' conclusions? - Which important parts of the explanation still lack evidence? One paper may inform several components, and several papers may provide different parts of the same explanation. For example, one study may establish a change in environmental conditions, another an organismal response, and another the consequence for the outcome being explained. Record the contribution that each paper actually makes without extending it to the entire explanation. ## Write working synthesis statements A **working synthesis statement** records a conclusion that the combined literature currently supports. It is a tool for comparing evidence and exposing uncertainty. Its wording can remain rough because it is not yet a topic sentence. For each component of the explanation, record: - A working synthesis statement. - The studies and findings that support it directly. - Evidence that conflicts with or qualifies it. - The organisms, places, time periods, and levels of observation represented by the evidence. - Differences in measurement or study design that affect comparison. - The assumptions or limits on the conclusion. - Additional evidence that would strengthen, narrow, or overturn it. Aim for an accurate statement of the current evidence rather than the strongest possible generalization. A finding reported secondhand can help locate the original paper, while the original paper should supply the evidence used in the synthesis. ### Example: nest success and predation risk Consider three studies from the reference literature: - Stracey (2011) found that the abundance of potential nest predators did not correspond closely to nest-predation rates in urban and non-urban habitats. Predator identity, prey switching, and nest defense provided possible explanations. - Sperry et al. (2012) connected seasonal rat-snake activity to seasonal nest survival and showed why breeding timing and nest-site selection could change that relationship among bird species. - Perry et al. (2008) found lower predation at nests farther inside Least Flycatcher clusters, a pattern consistent with predator deterrence. A working synthesis statement might be: > Nest-predation risk depends on which predators are active, when and where birds encounter them, and how birds respond to them. Total potential-predator abundance alone may obscure these processes. The three studies contribute different parts of that statement. They do not test one shared mechanism or use a common measure of predation risk. The synthesis therefore supports the importance of predator identity, activity, exposure, and defense while preserving uncertainty about which mechanism matters in a particular system. The next search could target studies that measure predator identity or activity together with nest fate. That search would test how widely the synthesis applies and whether one proposed process has stronger support than the others. ## Test each synthesis statement Evaluate each working statement before carrying it forward: 1. Which evidence supports the statement directly? 2. Are multiple citations based on independent studies or the same underlying dataset? 3. Does each source support the attached claim, or does it only cite another source for that finding? 4. Are conflicting results represented fairly? 5. Does the statement stay within the organisms, places, time periods, and levels of observation represented by the evidence? 6. Do differences in measurement make the studies difficult to compare? 7. What evidence would make the statement narrower, broader, or untenable? Revise the statement, qualify its scope, or return to searching when the evidence does not support it adequately. Retaining a visible disagreement is more useful than forcing a consensus that the studies do not provide. ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Now you!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} **Identify the synthesis** Which statement synthesizes evidence rather than listing studies?
::: ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Now you!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} **Build a set of synthesis notes** 1. Select two to four components from the QHP and the literature-synthesis table. 2. Group the relevant studies under each component. A study may appear in more than one group. 3. Write one working synthesis statement for each component. 4. Attach the direct evidence, conflicting evidence, organisms, places, time periods, measurements, and limits on the conclusion to each statement. 5. Identify the part of each statement that rests on the strongest assumption. 6. List any targeted searches or full-text reading needed to evaluate the statement. 7. Revise the QHP when the synthesis changes the plausible mechanism, expected pattern, or appropriate scope. ::: The completed synthesis notes provide the evidence needed to evaluate possible gaps in [Gap hunting](gap_hunting.qmd). They also supply the material used to determine paragraph jobs and construct a writing outline in [The four-stage outline process](writing_outlines.qmd). **Stopping point:** You can state what the literature currently supports for each component of the explanation, identify the evidence and limits attached to each statement, represent important disagreements, and name the searches or reading still needed. Paragraph decisions remain for the four-stage outline process.
